subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Lesson 3: Functions of Media Management in Advertising

subjective.question: Define media and mass media.
subjective.answer: Media is a tool used for storing and delivering information or data; the word is the plural of 'medium'. The term 'mass media' was coined in the 1920s for the segment of the media designed to reach very large audiences. It includes newspapers, magazines, books, radio, television and the newer electronic media that carry messages to mass audiences.

subjective.question: Explain the main functions of management as applied to a media organization.
subjective.answer: The main functions are planning, organizing, leading (directing), co-ordinating and controlling. Planning is the base function: managers decide in advance what is to be done, and it covers the business mission, objectives, policies and strategies. Organizing arranges people and resources to carry out the plan, directing/leading guides and motivates the staff, and controlling is a continuous process that checks performance against the plan and corrects deviations. In a media organization these functions are applied to gathering, producing and distributing content for mass audiences.

subjective.question: What is a communication plan? Write its main components.
subjective.answer: A communication plan is the document through which an organization plans how it will communicate with its audiences. Its key components are: (1) the target audiences to be reached, (2) the key messages to be delivered, (3) the budget available for the communication activities, and (4) a calendar or schedule of activities. Together these elements turn the organization's communication goals into an organized, practical programme.

subjective.question: What is a media strategy? Describe its six steps.
subjective.answer: A media strategy is a plan of action designed by an advertiser to bring advertising messages to the attention of the target consumers. Its six steps are: (1) Think it Through - analyze the market, product and audience before acting; (2) Write it Down - put the plan in written form; (3) Build Your Own Plan - tailor the plan to your own business instead of copying others; (4) Expect the Unexpected - keep flexibility for sudden changes; (5) Always Evaluate - measure the results of the plan; and (6) Build Your Draft Media Plan - prepare the working draft that selects media, timings and budgets for the campaign.

subjective.question: Explain the three strategies through which a business can achieve geometric growth.
subjective.answer: A business can grow geometrically by combining three strategies: (1) increasing the number of customers, (2) increasing the average transaction size, so each customer spends more per purchase, and (3) increasing the frequency of repurchase, so customers buy more often. Working on any one strategy gives only arithmetic growth, but when all three improve together their effects multiply, producing geometric (rapid, compounding) growth.

subjective.topic: Lesson 3: Functions of Media Management in Advertising
subjective.question: Differentiate between a media planner and a media buyer.
subjective.answer: The media planner studies the market and the target audience and decides which media (newspapers, television, radio, magazines, outdoor, etc.) will carry the advertisements, in what combination and at what times, so that the message reaches the right people most effectively. The media buyer implements that plan: he or she negotiates with media owners and buys the actual space and time at the best possible rates and positions. In short, the planner selects the media; the buyer purchases them.

subjective.topic: Lesson 3: Functions of Media Management in Advertising
subjective.question: What is the difference between a rating point and a target rating point?
subjective.answer: A rating point represents one percent of the whole universe of households or people being measured, for example all television households in a market. A target rating point (TRP) represents one percent of a specific segment of that universe - the advertiser's target audience, such as women aged 18-35. Ratings therefore measure total reach, while target rating points measure reach within the particular group the advertiser wants to influence.

subjective.topic: Lesson 3: Functions of Media Management in Advertising
subjective.question: Describe the five stages in the development of global advertising.
subjective.answer: As advertisers expand beyond their home markets, global advertising develops through five stages: (1) Domestic - advertising is confined to the home country; (2) Export - the home agency handles advertising in export markets; (3) International - local agencies or branches are used abroad; (4) Multi-national - campaigns are planned regionally for groups of countries; and (5) Global - a single worldwide strategy and campaign theme is used across all markets.

subjective.question: What is media ethics? What is the 'canons of journalism'?
subjective.answer: Media ethics is the subdivision of applied ethics concerned with the moral principles and standards that govern the conduct of media professionals. In journalism, these standards are expressed in a code of ethics, also called the canons of journalism. They cover accuracy, fairness, honesty, respect for privacy, avoidance of harm and conflicts of interest, and accountability to the public. Because the media enjoy freedom and power, ethical codes answer the classic question: 'Who guards the guardians?'

subjective.question: Differentiate between slander and libel.
subjective.answer: Both slander and libel are forms of defamation - false statements that damage a person's reputation. Slander is spoken defamation: the damaging statement is made orally, for example in a broadcast comment or speech. Libel is written or published defamation: the damaging statement appears in print, in a broadcast script or in another lasting form. Because libel is recorded and widely circulated, it is generally treated as the more serious offence in media law and ethics.

subjective.question: Define media bias and discuss its major types.
subjective.answer: Media bias is the prejudice or perceived bias of journalists and news producers within the mass media, shown in the selection of events and stories that are reported and in how they are covered. Its major types include ethnic and racial bias, ideological bias, peer culture bias, political bias, corporate bias, sensationalism and bias of ease or expediency. Commercial pressure also produces bias: because advertisers are the media's real customers and the audience is the product sold to them, content may favour advertisers' interests.

subjective.question: How does bias appear through placement, headlines and word choice in news media?
subjective.answer: Bias can enter news without changing the basic facts. Through placement, stories an editor favours are put on the front page or at the top of a bulletin, while others are buried inside. Through headlines - the most-read part of a newspaper - a slanted headline can colour the whole story. Bias also appears through the choice and cropping of photos, through the names and titles used for people and groups, through selective statistics, through source control (deciding who is quoted), and through word choice and tone in the story itself.

subjective.question: What is convergence in media technology? Explain with an example.
subjective.answer: Convergence is the coming together of previously separate communication technologies into a single coordinated system - in the handouts it is illustrated by the coordination of the computer and the television set to create a new medium. Driven by the semiconductor chip and digitization, convergence blurs the boundaries between broadcasting, computing and telecommunications, so that text, sound and video can be produced, stored and delivered through one device or network.

subjective.question: Differentiate between teletext and videotext (videotex).
subjective.answer: Teletext is a one-way information service transmitted over the air together with the ordinary television signal, using the unused lines of the vertical blanking interval; the viewer selects pages with a decoder but cannot respond - examples are the BBC's Ceefax and ITV's Oracle. Videotext (videotex) is delivered by wire, usually through the telephone network, and is interactive: the user can request information and send responses, as in British Telecom's Prestel, the world's first public videotex service, and Canada's Telidon system.

subjective.question: Describe the organizational structure of a newspaper's editorial division.
subjective.answer: A newspaper organization is divided into two main divisions: the business division and the editorial division. The editorial side is headed by editors with distinct roles: the managing editor supervises the overall news operation; the city editor is responsible for local news coverage; the news editor decides the placement and display of stories; and the wire editor handles copy received from news agencies such as AP and UPI. Reporters are of three kinds: general assignment reporters who cover any story given to them, beat reporters who regularly cover a fixed institution or subject, and specialist reporters who report in depth on a particular field.

subjective.question: What is PEMRA? Write its establishment, functions and licence categories.
subjective.answer: The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) was established on 1 March 2002 under the PEMRA Ordinance 2002 to regulate private broadcast media and distribution services in Pakistan. Its functions include issuing licences for broadcast and distribution services, setting standards for programmes and advertisements, and enforcing the code of conduct. PEMRA issues licences in six categories: international, national, provincial, local/community, specific or specialized subject, and cable TV network licences, granted for periods of 5, 10 or 15 years.

subjective.question: Explain the relationship between television networks and their affiliated stations.
subjective.answer: In the network-affiliate system, the national networks (such as NBC, CBS and ABC) are program suppliers: they produce or purchase programs and supply them to local stations. The networks themselves are not licensed by the FCC - it is the local stations that hold licences. An affiliate is an independently owned local station that contracts with a network and carries its programs for about 60 percent of its schedule; roughly 65 percent of the schedule is network-fed, while the station fills the remaining time with local programs (about 5-10 percent) and syndicated programs (about 25-30 percent), selling its own advertising in the breaks.

subjective.question: Write a note on the equal opportunity rule and the fairness doctrine.
subjective.answer: The equal opportunity rule (Section 315 of the Communications Act) provides that if a station allows one candidate for an office to use its facilities, it must give equal opportunities to all other candidates for the same office. The fairness doctrine, introduced by the FCC in 1949, required stations to devote reasonable time to controversial issues of public importance and to air contrasting viewpoints on them. The fairness doctrine was eliminated by the FCC in August 1987, whereas the equal opportunity rule for candidates remained part of the law.

subjective.question: Discuss the contribution of Adolph S. Ochs to The New York Times.
subjective.answer: Adolph S. Ochs bought The New York Times in 1896, when its circulation was only about 9,000. Working under the credo 'To Give the News Impartially, Without Fear or Favor', he rebuilt the paper on accurate, complete and unbiased reporting instead of sensationalism. Within three years he gained majority control of the company, and by his death in 1935 the circulation had risen to about 465,000. Ochs showed that a newspaper could succeed commercially through quality and credibility rather than yellow journalism.

subjective.question: What are the main sources of newspaper revenue? Also explain the term 'news hole'.
subjective.answer: Newspapers earn income from two main sources: advertising and circulation (sales and subscriptions). Advertising provides the major share - about three-fourths of total income - divided among local advertising (about 60 percent), national advertising (about 10 percent) and classified advertising (about 25 percent). Circulation provides roughly the remaining 25 percent, with about 77 percent of copies home-delivered. Because advertising occupies on average about 60 percent of the newspaper's space, the space left for news is called the 'news hole'.

subjective.question: Trace the development of radio broadcasting from the telegraph to KDKA.
subjective.answer: Radio developed step by step from earlier inventions: Morse opened the first telegraph line in 1844; Bell demonstrated the telephone in 1876; Hertz showed that energy could be sent through the air without wires; and Marconi, who formed his wireless company in 1896, sent the first wireless signals across the Atlantic in 1901. Lee De Forest's audion (1906) made voice transmission practical. After the First World War, Frank Conrad's experimental station 8XK became KDKA, which made the inaugural broadcast on 2 November 1920 by announcing the Harding-Cox presidential election results - the beginning of regular radio broadcasting.

subjective.question: How did commercial advertising begin on radio? Explain with reference to WEAF.
subjective.answer: Commercial radio advertising began with station WEAF of AT&T in New York. In 1922 WEAF became the first station to sell advertising time, and on 28 August 1922 the Queensboro Corporation paid 100 dollars for a ten-minute spot - the first paid radio advertisement. The experiment succeeded: by 1926 WEAF was grossing about 750,000 dollars a year from advertising, and selling airtime became the economic foundation of broadcasting.

subjective.question: Discuss how dependence on advertising affects newspapers, with its advantages and disadvantages.
subjective.answer: Since the penny press era, newspapers have depended on advertising as their main source of revenue; today advertising fills 60 to 70 percent of the average newspaper's space and provides about 30 billion dollars a year in the United States. This dependence is a mixed blessing. On the positive side, advertising money pays for the costly news-gathering, sports and financial services readers enjoy; without it a daily paper might cost over a dollar at the newsstand and more than 500 dollars a year delivered. On the negative side, dependence discourages newspapers from dealing harshly with the business community that supports them, biasing publishers in favour of the values and interests of merchants and businesses.

subjective.question: Explain the FCC's 1984 deregulation of broadcast ownership limits.
subjective.answer: For many years the FCC limited a single owner to seven television stations, seven AM and seven FM stations, of which no more than five TV stations could be VHF. Under deregulation in 1984, the FCC under chairman Mark Fowler raised the limits to twelve television, twelve AM and twelve FM stations. Congress, however, insisted that no single owner should be able to reach more than 25 percent of the US population with its combined stations. The change set off a wave of buying and selling of broadcast stations and sharply raised station prices.

subjective.question: What is the magic-bullet theory? Discuss the research evidence that challenged it.
subjective.answer: The magic-bullet (hypodermic) theory held that mass media messages strike every member of the audience directly and uniformly, like a bullet or an injection, producing similar powerful effects on all - an assumption seemingly supported by the Payne Fund studies of movies and children (1929-1932). Later research disproved it: Cantril's study of the 1938 War of the Worlds broadcast showed that some listeners panicked while others did not; Lazarsfeld's election research showed information also flows through opinion leaders (two-step flow); and Hovland's wartime film experiments showed films taught facts but did not change attitudes. Effects were shown to vary because of selective attention, selective perception and selective retention - audiences are active, not passive targets.

subjective.question: Explain the two-step flow theory of mass communication.
subjective.answer: The two-step flow theory, which emerged from Lazarsfeld, Berelson and Gaudet's study of the 1940 US presidential election, holds that information does not always flow directly from the media to the whole audience. In the first step, information flows from the mass media to certain people who follow the media closely; in the second step, these people - the opinion leaders - pass the information, along with their own interpretations, to a wider circle of people who depend on them. Thus interpersonal relationships and discussion play a significant role in the mass communication process.

subjective.question: What is content analysis? Explain with examples.
subjective.answer: Content analysis is one of the five basic approaches of mass media research. Its goal is to describe the content of communication objectively, systematically and quantitatively. Researchers define categories and count their occurrence in media content - for example, the number of men and women in major roles in prime-time television series, the number of violent acts in Saturday-morning cartoons, or the amount of newspaper space given to each presidential candidate in the week before an election. Because it works on the message itself, content analysis reveals patterns in media content that casual observation would miss.

subjective.question: Define public relations according to Public Relations News. What did John Marston add to it?
subjective.answer: Webster's defines public relations as 'the business of inducing the public to have understanding for and goodwill toward a person, firm, or institution'. The widely accepted Public Relations News definition is fuller: public relations is the management function which evaluates public attitudes, identifies the policies and procedures of an individual or organization with the public interest, and plans and executes a program of action to earn public understanding and acceptance. John Marston refined it by adding 'and communication'. In essence, public relations is planned, two-way communication through which an organization wins the understanding, acceptance, support and cooperation of its publics.

subjective.question: Discuss the contribution of Ivy Ledbetter Lee to modern public relations.
subjective.answer: Ivy Ledbetter Lee, called the father of modern public relations, held that the key to public acceptance of business was an honest information program, not suppression of bad news. In 1906, working for the anthracite coal industry, he issued his famous 'Declaration of Principles' to newspaper editors, promising that his bureau was not secret, that all work was done in the open, that he aimed to supply accurate news, and that editors would be helped to verify any statement of fact. He also developed the written handout to assist reporters, and his work for the Rockefeller family converted a name hated by the public into one of the nation's outstanding philanthropic sources.

subjective.question: List and briefly explain the traditional activities included in the public relations function.
subjective.answer: Public relations is a group of activities, not a single act. The traditional activities of the PR function include: publicity (placing newsworthy information in the media); opinion research (polls and surveys to take the pulse of the public); press agentry and special events management; promotion and fund-raising; lobbying (petitioning government in the client's interest); public affairs (political, educational and civic service in the community); institutional advertising (selling ideas or images); gift giving (screening and recommending grants); creating the printed voice of the institution (speeches, reports and brochures); and counseling management on courses of action. No single activity alone is public relations; together they perform the full function.

subjective.question: Explain the five stages of the adoption process given by Rogers and Shoemaker.
subjective.answer: According to Rogers and Shoemaker, an innovation spreads through five stages. (1) Awareness: the individual learns of the innovation's existence but lacks detailed information. (2) Interest: he develops interest and seeks additional information. (3) Evaluation: he uses the information to assess the innovation's applicability to his present and expected future situation. (4) Trial: if possible, he applies the new idea on a small scale to determine its utility. (5) Adoption: he actually acquires and uses the new item or idea continuously on a full scale. When many individuals adopt it and it comes into common use, diffusion of the innovation has occurred, and the mass media play a key role by spreading awareness quickly and widely.

subjective.question: What is agenda-setting? Give examples of its operation.
subjective.answer: Agenda-setting is the idea, expressed by Maxwell McCombs and Don Shaw, that the media do not tell people what to think, but they do tell people what to think about. By selecting and emphasizing certain issues, the media transfer the importance of those issues to the public agenda. For example, media coverage of the civil rights movement in the 1960s placed racial injustice high on the public agenda and helped produce the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the Washington Post's coverage of the 1972 Watergate break-in set the national agenda; and television's pictures of the Ethiopian famine (the 'CNN Effect') moved a faraway issue into domestic public concern and triggered a massive relief effort.

subjective.question: Explain the theory of accumulation of minimal effects with examples.
subjective.answer: The theory of accumulation of minimal effects explains the media's long-range influence on social and cultural change. Although the impact of any single message on any one person may be minimal, continuous presentation of information about an issue over an extended period gradually adds up: increasing numbers of individuals slowly modify their beliefs and orientations, until society itself changes. Television's coverage of the civil rights movement in the 1960s built support for reform legislation; sustained media coverage gradually eroded American support for the Vietnam War; and the twenty-five-year media campaign against smoking changed public thinking and produced tough new laws on the habit.
